## TL;DR

Claude Codeâs multi-agent /code-review max caught 23 of 27 serious bugs on hard pull requests, against 21 for a single agent, but cost about $21 a review instead of 11 cents and took 56 minutes instead of 40 seconds.

- The trade-off. Two more bugs is close to this benchmarkâs noise, and the multi-agent review also made twice as many claims you have to read. Still, one serious bug in production can cost far more than $21, so it comes down to what a missed bug costs your team.

- How I measured it. 20 hard pull requests from a public benchmark, with Sonnet 5.5 doing the work in both settings to keep the bill manageable.

- What Iâd do. Start with /code-review high on Opus 5.5: across all 50 benchmark PRs it caught 51 of 66 serious bugs for about 36 cents each. If you run max , read its transcript to see which subagents actually ran, because some of mine skipped verification to stay under budget.

Anthropicâs Claude Code team has written down how it reviews code : several agents look for bugs at once, âthen a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree itâs real.â Anthropicâs Deputy CISO, Jason Clinton, calls narrow review agents âmuch more effective than one mega-prompt or super security agent.â Those posts are about Anthropicâs managed service and its internal process, and neither gives a count of the bugs the agents find or miss per pull request, how much else they say, how long a review takes or what it costs. The local /code-review command that ships with Claude Code, which in the teamâs words âruns a lighter version locallyâ, has the same shape at its max setting and is the one anyone can run, so I measured it.

I ran Claude Codeâs local /code-review command, not Anthropicâs managed Code Review service 1 , with one agent and with its multi-agent fan-out, scored both on 20 pull requests from a public benchmark 5 , and put them against Quickchat Review, the reviewer I built 4 . The benchmarkâs own score put the three leading reviews within 0.8 points of each other, so I also had two AI judges compare the reviews head to head 10 .

With its agents on Sonnet 5.5, the fan-out does catch bugs. It does not catch all of them, it takes most of an hour, it adds twice as many claims that the answer key does not list, and it cost $20.95 per finished review. 8 Quickchat Review works on the same idea, many narrow AI reviewers and a check before anything is posted. On Opus 5.5 the judgesâ ratings do not separate it from the fan-out, and it got there for $4.61 and 8.2 minutes per pull request, under a quarter of the fan-outâs recorded price per finished review and about a seventh of its wall-clock time under our concurrency and rate limits.

## What I measured

The product. Claude Code 2.1.303 1 and its local /code-review command , a skill bundled with the CLI that works on any plan and bills to your usage or API key; Anthropicâs managed Code Review service is a separate product I did not test.

How it ran. Headless, in a locked-down Docker sandbox with no GitHub token and no GitHub writes 2 :

claude -p '/code-review high <base>...<head>' --output-format json

In Claude Codeâs own transcripts, high and max select two different review recipes, and the documentation describes neither 3 . At high it starts one agent: high effort â 8 inline angles â dedup (no verify) â â¤10 findings . At max it fans out: max effort â 5+5 angles Ã 8 candidates â 1-vote verify â sweep â â¤15 findings , about ten finder agents, a verifier agent per candidate, then a sweep. To make max affordable on twenty PRs I forced every subagent onto Sonnet 5.5, capped each review at $30 and gave it 90 minutes 4 ; none of that is a shipped default, and neither are the rest of my settings 2 . The two recipes differ in more than their number of agents, so this compares the two settings Claude Code ships, not parallelism alone 3 .

The three review shapes compared in this post, each as its tool intends it.

The benchmark. Martianâs Code Review Bench : 20 of its 50 PRs from Sentry, Grafana, Cal.com, Discourse and Keycloak, scored by Martianâs own pipeline with one LLM judge, GPT-6.1 Sol, for every reviewer 7 . Its pipeline splits each review into claims and matches them against the key; a claim that matches nothing is an unmatched claim 7 . Twenty and not fifty because the full set of max reviews would have cost about $1,000 and run for about 16 hours 5 . The 20 are the PRs where Quickchat Review on two other models had done worst, a selection expected to favour every other reviewer; Claude Code high on Opus 5.5 and Quickchat Review on Sonnet 5.5 also ran on all 50 5 .

Costs and times. Claude Codeâs dollar figures are the estimates it records for each session, apart from one recount labelled where it appears, and Quickchat Reviewâs are computed from token usage, both at list prices; every time is wall-clock with several reviews running at once 8 9 . max has three cost figures, each labelled where it appears: $20.95 per finished review, $19.90 over all 20 PRs in the charts, and about $440 actually spent 8 .

## The fan-out matched two more serious issues than one agent

Both runs reviewed the same 20 PRs with Sonnet 5.5 doing the work 4 . The fan-out matched two more of the 27 serious answer-key issues and the same number of issues overall; two issues is about the scoring noise on this benchmark, so I cannot say whether that difference would repeat 7 . Match counts are totals over the 20 PRs and the other rows are means; the max columnâs time and cost rest on its 19 finished reviews, and its match and claim counts cover all 20, with the timed-out review counted as zero and five reviews scored from reports recovered from their transcripts 9 .

The fan-out still missed 4 of the 27 serious issues. It produced twice as many unmatched claims, and its recorded subtotal was 188 times one agentâs, $398.03 against $2.12 8 .

On the same 20 hard PRs with Sonnet 5.5, Claude Code max matched 2 more serious answer-key issues than high and the same number overall. The chartâs $19.90 a review spreads the recorded subtotal over all 20 PRs; per finished review it is $20.95.

## What happens inside a max review

The unforced configuration, on one small PR. On browser-use #857, a 97-line change with five defects in our answer key 6 , /code-review high on Opus 5.5 found all five in 70 seconds for 32 cents. max with Opus 5.5 on every agent 4 started 9 finder agents and 14 verifiers, made 608 API calls and had spent $40.64 , by our recount of those calls 8 , when our 30-minute limit stopped it at 31 minutes. It printed nothing, because Claude Code prints the review only when it finishes.

Cumulative cost of the all-Opus 5.5 max run on browser-use #857 until the 30-minute limit stopped it with nothing printed, with the high run on Opus 5.5 as the dot near the origin.

The model running the recipe decides how much of it runs. Same max prompt, same PR, a different model forced onto the review agent and every child: Opus 5.5 launched 9 finders and 14 verifiers, Sonnet 5.5 launched 5 finders and no verifiers, and Haiku 5.5 launched no finders and 5 verifiers 6 . The Sonnet run cost $13.31 and took 32 minutes, the Haiku run $0.53 and 13.5 minutes, and both found all five defects. Each is a single run, and the Sonnet and Haiku runs had a $15 budget cap the agents could see, while the Opus run had none 6 .

Opus 5.5 launched nearly all of the max recipe and printed nothing before the limit, while Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 each skipped part of it and still found all five defects.

Agents cut work when they can see the budget. Five of the 19 finished max reviews launched no verifier at all. The agents can see a running budget line in their context, and four of the five named it as the reason, one in these words: âPer-candidate verifier agents were skipped because of budget.â 3 No review reached the $30 cap, so an uncapped max might run more verifiers and cost more 3 .

Cost did not track PR size. Finished reviews cost $15.17 to $26.09 each, with only a weak association with changed lines (r = 0.18) 8 .

Claude Code max with Sonnet 5.5 agents spent $15 to $26 on every finished hard PR, close to the $30 cap it could see, while high on Sonnet 5.5 stayed between six and sixteen cents.

The verifier checks that a bug is real, not that the PR introduced it. In the all-Opus max run on browser-use #857 the verifiers assessed 18 candidate bugs, marked 16 confirmed and 2 plausible, and refuted none; two of the confirmed bugs existed before the PR 6 .

Several reviews exited successfully without a usable report. Five of the twenty max reviews returned a closing note instead of the review, for example: âThe last background agents have finished. The report above stands, with no findings to add or remove.â Those five PRs delivered 2 of their 63 findings. One review ran into the 90-minute limit without a report, and 25 of 339 agents died on rate-limit errors from our API key, 23 of them inside 11 reviews that still reported success, so a check of the exit status alone would have missed all of this 9 .

## The answer key could not separate the leaders

The answer key did rank the reviews: max scored 30.0 on the benchmarkâs F2, well below the leaders. It did not separate the leaders: Quickchat Review on Sonnet 5.5 at 43.9, Claude Code high on Opus 5.5 at 43.2 and Claude Code high on Sonnet 5.5 at 43.1, three very different setups within 0.8 points. Martianâs key holds about 3.7 entries per PR, the reviews made 8 to 26 claims per PR, and the key cannot tell a true claim it lacks from a wrong one 7 .

So I added a second instrument: a judge that reads two reviews of the same PR side by side, with the diff, the touched files and the answer key, and says which one a maintainer would rather receive, with a verdict each for recall, precision, finding quality and writing 10 . Two judges from different providers, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, rated 298 matchups each with identical prompts 10 , and the results are on the Elo scale, over the reviews that exist 11 .

## What the judges found

The judges rated the fan-out highest, though not clearly above Quickchat Review on Opus 5.5. The five main configurations on the same 20 PRs:

Match counts are totals over the 20 PRs, unmatched claims are means over all 20, and time and cost are means, for max over its 19 finished reviews 8 . Rows on the same model compare complete configurations, which differ in more than the harness; Quickchat Review also ran six quality passes on GPT-6 Luna, under 2% of its cost 4 .

The review the answer key scores last, Claude Code max with Sonnet 5.5 agents, is the one the judges rate highest.

The judges credited max with findings the answer key does not list: over their 194 recall verdicts on its pairs it won 162, tied 22 and lost 10. It also came last on writing, with 14 wins against 179 losses 11 . Against high on Opus 5.5 it rates +148 (95% interval +64 to +241), about a 70% expected win rate under the fitted model, at 61 times the recorded cost; that margin comes mostly from the Opus judge, and the GPT judge on its own does not separate the two 11 . It rates 38 points above Quickchat Review on Opus 5.5, with a 95% interval from â33 to +135: the interval includes zero, so these data do not say which of the two is better 11 .

Among the five main setups, the judges rate Claude Code max with Sonnet 5.5 agents best at finding problems and worst at precision and at writing them up.

The two judges agreed on precision 76% of the time and on recall 70%, but on the overall winner only 56%, and each judgeâs highest-rated configuration ran on its own model family 12 . GPT favoured lean reviews and Opus thorough ones, so the overall ranking rests on how much a missed bug weighs against a wasted comment; the recall, precision and writing verdicts are where the two jud

## Intro

Setting long-running tasks for AI Agents to work on computers is the way to work in 2026. I have 15-20 Claude Code / Codex agents running for me every day. I wanted to see if they can do useful work for me in the realm of chess training.

At my chess level, you have to have some kind of an opening repertoire. Even if you spend ~0h per week actually training chess. You do find yourself often falling into trouble in similar kinds of positions. I wanted Claude to go ahead and do two things for me:

- Find 5-10 positions I often misplay

- Explain to me how to do better in those positions in a way digestible for a 2000-2200 ELO player (not grandmaster- or engine-speak)

I found both Claudeâs results and process quite impressive so Iâm sharing them here. Key elements that caught my attention:

- the scoring system Claude devised for detecting and ranking teachable positions

- how it calibrated findings to my playing strength

- the actual 9 positions it ended up highlighting

## What I did

I used Claude Code and Stockfish 19 on a two-core Linux VM to go through 2,000 of my chess.com blitz games, find the Pirc and Kingâs Indian positions I keep going wrong in, and turn the result into an eleven-page PDF brochure written for a 2000 to 2200 player. The session ran for four hours and thirteen minutes on its own while I was at home with the laptop closed, and I checked on it from my phone.

The nine positions and what I learned from them are in What I learned about my chess . The brochure itself is a PDF you can download .

## Why the Pirc and the Kingâs Indian keep getting me into trouble

As Black I have played the Pirc against 1.e4 and the Kingâs Indian against 1.d4 for a very long time. Both give good counterattacking chances and both are on thin ice as was once explained to me by GM Mateusz Bartel . White plays simple, natural moves, I make one small inaccuracy, and by move 15 or 20 I am close to lost. It happens far less than it used to, but it still happens, and I had a feeling it happened in the same handful of positions.

## Isnât a chess engine or chess.com enough?

At my level, learning openings from engine recommendations makes no sense. You will learn what the best move is but wonât understand why and how to proceed. Itâs almost as bad as writing blog posts using AI.

chess.comâs Game Review is fun but itâs aimed at beginner players and its suggestions are very basic. I wonder if the team at chess.com is working on making Game Review better calibrated to individual playerâs strength?

By far the best way to train chess is with a coach or with chess books. But that takes a lot of time. So letâs use AI instead.

Position 6 of the brochure , rendered from its data: the Austrian Attack after 6.Be3 Ng4 7.Bg1. I played 7â¦e5 in all three games that reached it. The engine wants 7â¦c5.

## What I wanted from 2,000 games

I wanted five to ten positions: the specific moments where my habits and the engine disagree, with the move I should play and the reason in words a 2200 player uses. No ocean of engine lines, and no advice to develop my pieces and castle early. A recurring-position audit is a run that groups every game by the exact position where my results start to slip, so the positions are ranked by how often I reach them and how much they cost, not by how badly one game went.

Doing that by hand means loading hundreds of games into an analysis board, noting the move where the evaluation drops, and keeping a tally. It is weeks of evenings, which is why nobody does it.

## Why run this as an unattended Claude Code session on a VM?

These days I only ever work with ten to twenty AI sessions running at the same time, so doing this project the same way was the natural choice. Each session gets its own virtual machine, which changes three things. It can run for hours without my laptop being open. It can install whatever it needs, in this case a PDF typesetter and two fonts. And it can be reached from a phone , because the terminal is a web page.

The machine for this run had two CPU cores, 4 GB of memory, Stockfish 19 and the python-chess library already installed, and a Claude Code session that starts with permission prompts switched off. The VM does not idle or sleep, which matters when the engine is going to run for three and a half hours. It also does not notify you when the work is done; if you want a ping, you ask for one, and I did.

## What was the first prompt?

The first message asks for a plan, not for work. It states who I am, what I want, what the machine has, how long it may run, and what the deliverable is. It also contains the one rule that let me publish this post: my username and my opponentsâ names stay out of everything it prints.

I'm a 2200+ blitz player on chess.com. As Black I play the Pirc and the King's Indian. They give good counterattacking chances but they're risky: White plays simple natural moves, I make one small inaccuracy, and by move 15-20 I'm close to lost. It happens less than it used to, but it still happens, and I want to know exactly where. I want you to go through all my games and find the 5-10 positions where this keeps happening, then teach me those positions. What you have here: Stockfish 19, python-chess in .venv, 2 CPU cores and 4 GB of RAM. My chess.com username is in /home/dev/chess/.chesscom_username. Read it from there and never print it. I'm going to publish screenshots of this session, so keep my username, my opponents' names and anything about the hosting of this machine out of logs, filenames, printed output and the report. Call my opponents "White". I think I have about 1,900 blitz games. Keep the ones where I'm Black and the opening is the Pirc, the King's Indian or the Modern. Classify by the actual move sequence, not only by the ECO code chess.com attaches. What I want at the end is a PDF brochure in results/. Page one is a one-pager: the positions at a glance. Then one page per position with a diagram from my side of the board, the line that gets there, what I usually play there and how often (from my own games), what I should play instead, and why, in the words a 2000-2200 FIDE player would use. No beginner advice. No pages of engine lines. If a move is only good for reasons Stockfish finds at depth 30, I can't learn it; prefer plan-level explanations and say when the engine's reason is not a human reason. Make it look good: this is something I want to print and keep. You can run for several hours and I won't be watching, so budget the engine time for two cores, save intermediate results so nothing is lost if something crashes, and keep a short progress file in reports/ that I can read from my phone. I did a planning session earlier and saved its notes in pipeline/DESIGN.md. Use them as a starting point, but it's your plan: check what holds up and change what doesn't. Before you run anything, write me a plan: how you'll download and classify the games, how you'll find the mistakes with the engine within the time budget, how you'll decide which positions make the cut, how you'll make sure the advice is pitched at my level and not a beginner's, and how you'll check your own work. Don't start until I say go.

The desktop browser at 19:03: the workspace page with its tabs, and the terminal with the first message just sent. Click to read it at full size; the text is the block above.

âSay when the engineâs reason is not a human reasonâ is what separates a brochure for me from a brochure for a computer. The planning note the prompt mentions, pipeline/DESIGN.md , is a file from an earlier session: about 5,000 words of measurements and arithmetic, with the engine speed on this machine, the node budgets, the scoring ideas and the privacy rules. It opens like this:

> Design note: finding my recurring Pirc / Kingâs Indian trouble spots. Written in a planning session on 2026-10-03. It records what was measured on this machine and the approach that came out of that planning. It is a starting point, not a spec. Check the numbers, change what does not hold up, and present your own plan before running anything.

Its decision table, which the session kept almost unchanged apart from the budgets:

The full note is published next to the brochure. Handing the next session a file is cheaper than typing the same context twice, and it is also what let the sessionâs plan come back in five minutes.

## What did Claude Code plan?

The plan came back five and a half minutes later , in seven numbered sections and about 1,200 words. It covered the download and the classification, an engine budget in nodes rather than seconds, the selection rules, how it would keep the advice at my level, how it would check its own work, what it had changed from my notes, and a timeline. I was supposed to read it on the laptop before leaving, and I did.

The end of the plan, captured in the desktop browser at 19:10: the timeline table, the deliverables and the assumptions it wanted confirmed.

The planâs estimates and what actually happened:

I sent two small adjustments and said go. The reply confirmed both and started installing the typesetter in the background while it wrote the first scripts.

## How Claude Code downloaded and classified 2,000 chess.com games

The chess.com public API serves a playerâs games as monthly archives, 29 of them in my case, with the full PGN of every game. The download took 41 seconds : 2,000 games, 1,904 of them 3+2 blitz, 955 of those with me as Black.

Download and classification output, rendered from the session transcript.

Classification was by move sequence, not by the opening name chess.com attaches. A game counts as mine if Black plays both â¦d6 and â¦g6 in the first ten moves and does not push â¦d5 or an early â¦c5; it is a Kingâs Indian if White has both c4 and d4 by move 10, and a Pirc if White has e4 without c4. That gave 791 games: 532 Pirc and 259 Kingâs Indian . The classifier was cross-checked against chess.comâs labels afterwards and kept 99 percent of the games chess.com calls Pirc and 92 percent of the ones it calls Kingâs Indian. My Modern Defense bucket stayed empty, because I play â¦Nf6 early in every game.

Two facts came out of this stage before any engine ran. I score 54 percent in the Pirc and 49 percent in the Kingâs Indian. And a bigger gap: after move 12 my expected score is 40 percent or less in 43 percent of my Kingâs Indian games, against 28 percent of my Pirc games . The thin ice was mostly on the 1.d4 side. I would have guessed the opposite.

## How Stockfish screened 791 games on two cores

The engine work was three passes with fixed node budgets, so that a throttled core would stretch the clock without changing a result. Before launching, the session ran a smoke test, measured about 170,000 nodes per second per core, less than my notes had assumed, and cut the budgets to fit: 100,000 nodes per position for screening and 600,000 for confirmation .

Concept diagram of the pipeline. Every box is a script the session wrote during the run; the cache in the middle is what makes it resumable.

The unit of work was a position, not a game. Opening positions repeat heavily within one playerâs repertoire, so every position was stored once under its FEN in a small SQLite cache, keyed by the budget it was analysed at. Everything downstream (the per-game tables, the error list, the clusters, the brochure) is computed from that cache plus the raw games. Any stage can be re-run at any time, and a crash costs one position.

The screening pass covered moves 4 to 20 of every game in two phases: 9,155 unique positions out of 14,203 raw ones in the first, 11,563 in the second, with games already decided by move 12 skipped in the second. 20,718 positions in 91 minutes , two single-threaded engine workers, median depth 15, half a second each.

The screening pass under way, rendered from the session transcript. The progress file was rewritten ever

A Discord FAQ and feedback bot answers product questions from your documentation and records membersâ explicit submissions in Google Sheets. It can also collect questions the docs cannot answer and flag conversations that need a person.

This tutorial builds that workflow in Quickchat AI for Beacon Labs , a fictional SDK company. You will configure a Knowledge Base, two AI Actions, and Human Handoff. The source articles, prompts, request bodies and test messages are included, so you can reproduce the setup without writing or hosting a bot service.

The recipe treats âPlease submit a feature request for CSV export so I can prepare weekly reportsâ as an instruction to record the request immediately. The team reviews it afterward. The testing and tuning examples show how to check the saved records, handle failed writes, and improve the Agentâs decisions.

## What does the Discord bot do?

The memberâs intent determines which of four routes the Agent should take. Each route has a different result to verify.

Concept diagram of the intended workflow. The recording Actions append to separate spreadsheet tabs.

The Agent responds when a member addresses it through supported Discord interactions. A fixed greeting can invite that conversation; it does not run the recording Actions. The Discord welcome bot guide covers that entry point.

## How does Discord connect to Google Sheets?

Discord carries the conversation, the Knowledge Base supplies product facts, and two AI Actions append structured records to a Google spreadsheet. Human Handoff keeps requests for a person in the teamâs Quickchat AI Inbox.

An Action has a fixed HTTP method, destination, and body template. The model decides whether to call it and fills the parameters you define. Quickchat AI supplies the token and conversation context when it sends the request.

The model chooses the content. The platform supplies the connection and conversation values. Check both the Action result and the saved row.

The Google Actions work with the shared one-click Discord connection because they use a Google credential. Discord administration Actions, such as creating private tickets or changing roles, need your own Discord bot credential and are a separate setup.

For feedback, the Main Prompt and Action description instruct the model to record a complete, explicit submission request. A valid Action call sends the request immediately. An ordinary question, quoted example or brainstorming message should produce no feedback row. Documentation-gap recording is automatic and also needs team review.

Required and No default address missing parameter values. They do not determine the memberâs intent, reject every meaningless value, or prove a record is complete. Compare the memberâs actual request, the Action parameters, and the resulting spreadsheet cells.

### What do you need before starting?

Use a dedicated demo Agent and a test channel so the exampleâs fictional content and records stay together.

- Create a Quickchat AI account . If you register with email and a password, open the verification link. Complete the setup flow and name the Agent Beacon Community Assistant . Free is for personal, non-commercial testing; a business community needs a commercial-use plan.

- Have a Google account ready to authorize the native Sheets connection. It will create the exampleâs spreadsheet. You do not need an existing workbook or an API key.

- Use a Discord server where you can authorize the bot and adjust its channel permissions. Reserve a text channel for testing. You will connect Discord before testing feedback submissions.

Download the Beacon demo kit for the five source articles, Main Prompt, JSON bodies, sheet headers, and test inputs. These are editable setup files, not a one-click import. The full prompt and source articles also appear at the end of this guide.

### What does this Discord bot cost?

The entry plans cover personal testing and commercial use:

Replies, AI Preview and Simulation Testing use credits. Consumption depends on the selected model, so include test runs in your budget. See Quickchat AI pricing for plan details.

## Can ChatGPT or Claude set up this Discord bot?

Yes, they can prepare most of the configuration through Quickchat AIâs account MCP connector. The assistant can create a dedicated Agent, save its Main Prompt, add knowledge articles, configure the two Actions, and prepare a Simulation Testing dataset. Your community then uses the Agent in Discord.

Open Manage your AI in above the dashboard sidebar to find these connection options. This is the real local dashboard.

- Open Quickchat AI in ChatGPT and choose Install plugin , or connect Quickchat AI from the Claude Directory . Sign in to the Quickchat AI account that will own the demo.

- Extract the demo kit linked above. Attach its text setup files, including the knowledge folder, or paste their contents into the conversation.

- Send the setup request below and review any approvals your AI app presents.

Use the Quickchat AI connector to prepare the Beacon Community Assistant from the attached demo kit. Inspect the available tools and my Agents first. Use an empty dedicated Agent or create one; leave my other working Agents alone. Show me the chosen Agent's name and ID. Save main-prompt.txt and the five knowledge articles verbatim. Configure record_community_feedback and record_documentation_gap exactly as sheets-recipe.md and the supplied descriptions and JSON bodies specify. Preserve AI decides, RAW append, the updatedRows response filter, null defaults for required parameters, and the empty-string default for optional partial_answer. After I authorize Google Sheets, read the native starter Action to obtain its spreadsheet URL. Turn that starter off without renaming it. Use the Google Sheets System Token placeholder. Keep the two reporting Actions inactive until both tabs and their headers are ready. Create the Beacon FAQ and gap checks dataset from simulation-messages.txt and simulation-rubric.txt, without running it. Give me the Discord authorization link to open myself and set Reply in channel to match this guide. Read back the saved configuration and list the browser steps I still need to complete. Do not run tests yet.

You still authorize Google Sheets , choose and approve the Discord server , and configure Human Handoff in the dashboard. The management connector also has no spreadsheet tab editor: create Feedback and Knowledge gaps and paste their headers in Sheets, or use a separately connected Sheets tool.

Once those steps are complete, check that the articles show Ready and ask the assistant to activate the two reporting Actions. You can then ask it to run selected test conversations or a Simulation dataset and inspect the replies and Action logs. These tests use credits and active Actions can write real rows.

The numbered steps below give you the exact settings to review, whichever setup route you choose. The account MCP guide also covers other compatible AI clients.

## Step 1: Add the product knowledge

Create five short articles so the Agent has enough knowledge to answer useful questions and one deliberate gap to discover.

- Open Knowledge Base â Add Article .

- In Create custom article , enter a title from the table below and click Create article .

- In the Edit Article drawer, paste the matching source into Content and click Save .

- Repeat for all five sources and wait until each shows Ready . Saving an individual article processes it; this flow does not require a separate Retrain or Deploy command.

Actual local Knowledge Base containing the five fictional source articles.

The package names and versions are teaching data; do not install the fictional packages. Create the four channels named in the channel-map source, or adapt that source to your test serverâs channel names.

Leave SAML out of these sources for the initial test. That missing information gives you a deliberate documentation gap to measure. Adding a made-up negative answer would remove it.

For your own product, replace these facts with approved documentation. The documentation-to-support-Agent tutorial covers importing a real public site.

## Step 2: Set the Agentâs Main Prompt

The Main Prompt connects the knowledge, submission, recording, and handoff rules into one conversation policy.

- Open Identity â Main Prompt .

- Paste the complete prompt from the copyable section below or main-prompt.txt in the download.

- Save it. Its Action names must match record_community_feedback and record_documentation_gap , which you will create next.

The opening of the current prompt in the real local editor. Paste the complete prompt from the appendix or download, including the workflow rules below this excerpt.

For feedback, the intended sequence is receive a complete submission request â append â acknowledge â team review . If details are missing, the Agent asks the member to send the complete request together in one message.

For a documentation gap, it checks each factual part of the question, records what remains unanswered, and preserves the supported answer. Neither a feedback row nor a gap record promises a release or a fix.

Before adding Actions, open AI Preview and ask Does JavaScript SDK 2.4 support Node.js 22? . Confirm that the reply uses the documented answer. If it does not, check the article contents and processing status before adding recording behavior.

## Step 3: Connect Google Sheets and prepare the tabs
